references.text: Jacob's blessing mentions 'him to whom it belongs' (Shiloh), a messianic prophecy about the coming one. John's question, 'Are you the one who is to come?', points to this expectation of a coming Savior.

'Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord' – the expression 'the one who comes' (ὁ ἐρχόμενος) in Luke 7:19 is closely linked to this messianic psalm about the one who comes in the name of the Lord.
Isaiah prophesies that God himself will come and save his people. John's question about Jesus being 'the one who is to come' reflects this expectation of God's saving arrival.
The prophecy that a Redeemer will come to Zion. John's question to Jesus is precisely whether he is this promised Redeemer.

Malachi prophesies that the Lord will suddenly come to his temple, and that a messenger will prepare the way before him. John the Baptist is this messenger, and his question concerns whether Jesus is the Lord whom Malachi prophesied about.
The parallel passage in Matthew where John the Baptist sends his disciples from prison to ask Jesus if he is 'the one who is to come'. This is the direct parallel to Luke 7:19.
The crowd cries out, 'Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord' at Jesus' entry into Jerusalem, thereby confirming that Jesus is 'the one who comes' whom John asked about.

The people wondered if John himself could be the Messiah, but John pointed further to someone stronger than him who was to come after him. The question in 7:19 follows up on this: Is Jesus truly this stronger one whom John had proclaimed?
The immediate continuation where the disciples bring John's question to Jesus, and Jesus answers by pointing to his miracles as signs that he is the one who was to come.

John the Baptist testifies about Jesus: 'Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!' John had already pointed out Jesus as the coming one, which gives depth to his later question from prison.
After the feeding miracle, the people say, 'This is truly the prophet who is to come into the world.' The title 'the one who comes' is here directly linked to Jesus after his miracles.

The Letter to the Hebrews quotes the prophecy: 'For yet a little while, and he that shall come will come, and will not tarry.' The expression 'the one who comes' is used here of Christ in light of messianic expectation.
